expected_evidence: astronomical: anomalous spikes in cosmogenic isotopes (14C, 10Be, 36Cl) in ice cores and tree rings consistent with a sudden burst of ionizing radiation around ~10,950 BCE (model-prior: this is the signature proposed for gamma-ray-burst hypotheses such as Melott & Thomas 2010, not confirmed data from the provided evidence set)

geological: ozone-depletion/nitrate concentration spikes in Greenland/Antarctic ice cores that would accompany atmospheric ionization from a gamma-ray event, distinct from the platinum/iridium/nanodiamond 'black mat' markers usually cited for a physical impactor
geological: stratigraphic dating of a distinct Younger Dryas boundary layer in North American sediments co-occurring in time with the isotopic anomaly
material: North American megafaunal death assemblages and archaeological (Clovis-era) site abandonment horizons clustering tightly around the same date
genetic: population bottleneck or extinction signatures in surviving North American fauna mtDNA/ancient DNA dated to the same interval
genetic/ecological: mutation-rate or radiation-damage signatures in surviving lineages that would specifically implicate ionizing radiation rather than climatic or impact-debris causes

model_prior: published literature proposing either an extraterrestrial impact (Firestone et al. 2007) or a nearby supernova/gamma-ray burst (Melott & Thomas 2010; Larsson et al.) as the Younger Dryas trigger — recalled from training data, unverified against the evidence text given here
response.rationale: The stated interval (-10950) aligns with the Younger Dryas onset, so the younger-dryas detectability row is the appropriate reference rather than any later period. The hypothesis is a hybrid: it invokes a 'cosmic-impact' actor but specifies a 'gamma-ray-ionization' mechanism, which in the scientific literature (model-prior, unverified: Melott & Thomas 2010, Larsson et al.) is actually a competing/alternative hypothesis to physical-impactor models (e.g., Firestone et al. 2007), not typically paired with 'impact' terminology. This internal tension matters for evidence expectations: a genuine impact would leave physical debris (iridium, platinum, nanodiamonds, spherules) in the geological record, whereas a gamma-ray-ionization event would instead leave isotopic/atmospheric-chemistry signatures (14C, 10Be, 36Cl, nitrate spikes) with no crater or debris field. Both classes of evidence are, in principle, well preserved over ~13,000 years — ice cores, varved sediments, and dated bone assemblages from the Younger Dryas boundary have survived and been extensively sampled by paleoclimatologists, so detection is plausible in principle (astronomical 0.7 and geological 0.65 detectability in the table support this). However, several factors reduce practical detectability below the raw table values: (1) the mechanism is doubly speculative (impact + ionization is not a standard combination), making any observed anomaly ambiguous between multiple candidate causes (solar event, impact debris, volcanism, meltwater pulse) rather than uniquely diagnostic of a gamma-ray-ionization event; (2) genetic evidence for extinction bottlenecks (0.3) and material archaeological evidence (0.35) are comparatively weak, since ancient DNA and site preservation from this period are sparse and often degraded; (3) attributing any isotopic spike specifically to ionizing radiation from a cosmic source, rather than to solar proton events or the well-documented Younger Dryas climate shift itself, requires resolving power the geochemical record may not provide even where it survives. Given plausible survival but genuine ambiguity/underdetermination in attribution, I lower the blended detectability somewhat below the raw astronomical/geological figures. An absence of a clean, unambiguous ionization signature should not be treated as strong disconfirmation, since the signal (if real) would likely be conflated with other Younger Dryas boundary phenomena already discussed in the literature.
